questions.title: Lambdas & Streams practice 1
questions.prompt: Which stream operation keeps only items that pass a condition?
choices: filter
map
count
toList
questions.explanation: Filter receives a condition and keeps values for which that condition is true. Map changes values instead of deciding whether to keep them.

questions.title: Lambdas & Streams practice 2
choices: [Ada, Grace]
[true, true]
questions.explanation: Map replaces each String with the Integer returned by `length()`. Ada has three characters and Grace has five.

questions.title: Trace Lambdas & Streams
questions.prompt: What output does this code produce? Enter each line in order.
questions.explanation: The filter keeps passing scores. The map adds five points to each remaining score. `toList` starts the work and gathers the results. The resulting output is '[77, 95]'.

questions.title: Lambdas & Streams practice 5
questions.prompt: What is wrong with `scores.stream().filter(score -> score >= 60);` on its own?
choices: Without a terminal operation like toList, the filter never actually runs
filter is not a real stream method
It modifies the original scores list in place
It always returns an empty list
questions.explanation: Stream steps like `filter` and `map` are lazy: they describe work but do nothing until a terminal operation such as `toList`, `count`, or `forEach` pulls the values through. The version with `.toList()` produces the result; the bare filter just builds and discards a pipeline. Streams never change the source list.

questions.title: Loop instead of stream
questions.prompt: When might a regular loop be clearer than a Java stream pipeline?
choices: Use a regular loop for changing state, early exits, detailed error handling, or many side effects.
Use a stream when a loop would make complex state clearer.
Use `map` when the goal is to keep or discard elements.
Use `filter` when the goal is to transform each element.
questions.explanation: A loop is often clearer when the work needs changing state, early exits, detailed error handling, or many side effects. Streams shine when data flows through a short, readable series of transformations.

questions.title: Small lambda
questions.prompt: What makes a lambda comfortable to read?
choices: Forget the terminal operation.
Use a lambda for one small action.
Put many side effects inside a stream pipeline.
Assume intermediate stream steps run immediately.
questions.explanation: A lambda should usually express one small action or decision. If it grows into several branches and side effects, a named method or loop gives the logic room and a clearer name.

questions.title: Reading stream steps
questions.prompt: How should a student mentally read a stream pipeline?
choices: Use a lambda so long that it hides the rule.
Change the source collection while streaming it.
Read a stream from top to bottom as data steps.
Use streams for error handling with many recovery paths.
questions.explanation: Read a stream from top to bottom as data passing through steps: filter keeps values, map changes values, and the terminal operation produces or performs the result. That mental model is better than treating it as a magic loop replacement.

questions.title: Filter versus map
questions.prompt: How do `filter` and `map` divide their jobs?
choices: Build a pipeline whose order no longer matches the data story.
Ignore readability because the stream is shorter.
Use `forEach` when a collected result is needed.
Use filter to keep and map to change.
questions.explanation: `filter` decides which elements stay in the stream. `map` transforms each remaining element into another value. Mixing those roles makes the pipeline harder to verify.

questions.title: Terminal operation
questions.prompt: Why does a stream pipeline need a terminal operation?
choices: Finish with a terminal operation.
Run independent slow operations sequentially by accident.
Treat a stream as reusable after a terminal operation.
Use a lambda when a named method would clarify intent.
questions.explanation: Intermediate stream steps are lazy; they describe work but do not complete it by themselves. A terminal operation such as `collect`, `count`, or `forEach` starts the pipeline and produces the final effect or value.

questions.title: Readability limit
questions.prompt: What should happen when a stream hides the real work?
choices: Mix filtering, mapping, and mutation in one step.
Choose a loop when the stream would hide the real work.
Assume parallel streams are always faster.
Hide null handling inside a long chain.
questions.explanation: Switch to a loop or named helper when the stream stops telling a clear data story. Readability matters more than using a modern feature, especially when classmates need to debug the same code.
